Talks in Rome this week between Lebanon and Israel are expected to focus on expanding pilot zones in south Lebanon, resolving border disputes, and advancing a new security framework. But achieving safety and sovereignty for Lebanon requires serious policy reconsideration in both Washington and Beirut. 



The Rome talks follow Lebanese President Joseph Aoun’s visit to Washington last month, the first by a Lebanese head of state since 2009. His most important job was to convince President Donald Trump that Israel’s continued attacks on south Lebanon will not lead to a durable peace. Official readouts of the meeting suggest that the chemistry between the two leaders, a matter of high importance to the U.S. president, was good. But it is by no means clear whether Aoun achieved his primary objective.

Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz and efforts to extract payments for safe passage — plus, more recently, the Houthis’ move to attack Saudi shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — have highlighted the risks of maritime chokepoints to global shipping and raised questions about the future for freedom of navigation. The impacts extend beyond the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea, so we asked five experts to consider the implications for several other crucial waterways: the Strait of Malacca, the Taiwan Strait, the Panama Canal, the Suez Canal, and the Turkish Straits.Read more below.Patrick M.
